analysis.one_liner: Adds a 1,000% excise tax on sales of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee with no action beyond its introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a tax equal to ten times the sale price on semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns that meet its definitions of assault weapons, and on magazines holding more than 10 rounds. The tax is charged when manufacturers, producers, or importers sell the item, so a $1,500 rifle would carry a $15,000 tax, making covered guns and magazines effectively unaffordable for most buyers. Purchases by the federal, state, or local governments are exempt, so police and other public agencies could still buy them. In practice the bill works like a ban on these weapons for the civilian market, done through the tax code rather than an outright prohibition.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to gun violence from semiautomatic rifles and pistols with high-capacity magazines, including people in schools, workplaces, and public spaces, gain if these weapons are priced out of the civilian market. Taxpayers generally also avoid costs tied to mass shootings. Gun owners who do not want these specific weapons are unaffected except through the broader market.

how_it_helps.text: The 1,000% tax makes covered weapons and large-capacity magazines roughly eleven times more expensive at the point of manufacture or import, which would take them out of reach for almost all civilian buyers [S3].

The bill covers semiautomatic rifles and pistols with detachable magazines and features like pistol grips or threaded barrels, semiautomatic shotguns with more than 5 rounds, devices that speed up firing, and any parts to assemble them [S3].
Government purchases are exempt, so police and other public agencies could still acquire these weapons [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Gun manufacturers, importers, and retailers lose their civilian market for the covered weapons and magazines. Lawful gun owners who want a covered firearm would pay roughly ten times the price or switch to non-covered designs. The tax is built into the sales price, so buyers ultimately bear it.

drawbacks.text: A 1,000% tax functions as a prohibition through the tax code, and its definitions reach many common semiautomatic pistols and rifles, so it would sharply restrict access for gun owners who never misuse them [S3].

The tax is collected when the manufacturer, producer, or importer sells the article, and applies to sales after enactment, meaning existing lawful owners keep their guns while the supply of covered items and spare magazines effectively ends [S3].
Bolt-action, lever-action, and .22 rimfire firearms, and tubular .22 magazines, are excluded, so the tax does not cover hunting-style guns most often used in hunting and rural shooting sports [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit, if it worked as written, would be a large reduction in civilian access to the weapon types most used in mass shootings. The cost falls on the firearms industry and on gun owners who want those specific designs, and the blunt 1,000% rate raises real questions about legality and about how much of the market would simply shift to just-outside-the-definition firearms. It is a prohibition by another name, and supporters and opponents would judge that trade differently.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Beyer introduced the bill on August 4, 2023, with 24 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the action history shows no further action for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill ended the 118th Congress with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The firearms industry and gun owners who want access to these weapons are better off, since nothing changed. The Ways and Means Committee leadership avoided a recorded vote on an assault-weapon tax, which was politically difficult for any member regardless of position.

for.name: Rep. Donald S. Beyer Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on August 4, 2023.

for.name: 26 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat and none was a Republican.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the 118th Congress.

against.name: Firearms industry and gun-rights groups
against.role: Opponents of restrictions on semiautomatic firearms and large-capacity magazines
against.what_they_did: Fought assault-weapon restrictions broadly, and no Republican supported the bill; no gun-industry or gun-rights organization backed it.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 26 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored the bill; it also never reached a vote where partisan splits would have been recorded.

industries.note: The 1,000% tax would erase their civilian market for covered rifles, pistols, shotguns, magazines, and even frames and receiver parts. The industry consistently opposes bans or punitive taxes on these products, which are a core, high-margin part of its sales.
The tax applies at manufacture and import, so retailers and importers would lose the covered product lines. Retailers often cite the broader effects of gun-control laws on overall sales.
Purchases by the United States and state or local governments are exempt from the tax, so police agencies could keep acquiring covered weapons at normal prices.
